title: GRADE: An emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations

extracted.subtask_short: Separating evidence certainty from recommendation strength
extracted.subtask_description: Separates two judgments often conflated: how certain we are that an estimated effect is close to the true effect (certainty/quality of evidence for a claim), and given that certainty, how strongly to act on the claim (strength of recommendation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four certainty (quality) categories with explicit epistemic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: High quality: 'Further research is very unlikely to change our confidence in the estimate of effect.' Moderate quality: 'Further research is likely to have an important impact on our confidence in the estimate of effect and may change the estimate.' Low quality: 'Further research is very likely to have an important impact on our confidence in the estimate of effect and is likely to change the estimate.' Very low quality: 'Any estimate of effect is very uncertain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual test: would a new study change the estimate?
rubrics_metrics.description: The operational test for whether a claim is 'strongly,' 'moderately,' or 'weakly' supported: ask what a well-conducted additional study would most likely do to the current estimate. If it would probably leave the estimate essentially unchanged, the claim is strongly supported (high certainty). If a new study could plausibly overturn the current point estimate or its direction, the claim is weakly supported (low/very low certainty) regardless of how many studies currently exist or how confidently the original authors state their conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-design starting point (RCT high, observational low)
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence starts at high quality; observational (non-randomized) evidence starts at low quality, reflecting the greater a priori risk of confounding and selection bias in the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study limitations (risk of bias) downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the individual studies contributing to the claim well-designed and well-executed (adequate randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, complete follow-up, and outcome reporting free of selective reporting)? Serious flaws in the studies underlying a claim downgrade certainty even if the claim's chain of reasoning is otherwise correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency of results downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the studies point in materially different directions or magnitudes without an identifiable explanation (e.g., different populations, doses, follow-up length)? Unexplained heterogeneity across the studies cited for a claim is direct evidence that the claim is not well pinned down by the body of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirectness of evidence downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the evidence about the actual population, intervention, comparator, and outcome the claim is being made about, or does it require an inferential bridge (e.g., surrogate outcome standing in for a patient-important outcome, or a different population than the one the claim targets)? Any such gap between 'what was studied' and 'what is claimed' downgrades certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprecision downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the confidence interval around the pooled/study estimate narrow enough, and the sample/event count large enough, to rule out both a null effect and an effect of the opposite or much larger/smaller magnitude than claimed? Wide intervals mean the claim's specific magnitude (or even its direction) is not actually pinned down by the cited evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/reporting bias downgrade domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there reason to think unfavorable or null studies were not published or not reported, biasing the visible evidence base toward the claim being tested? This is a threat to the very existence of the evidence a claim relies on, not just its internal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upgrading criteria for observational evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large magnitude of effect (a very large or very consistent effect size is harder to explain away via plausible confounding alone). Dose-response gradient (if the outcome varies systematically with the dose/intensity of exposure, this is evidence for a causal, not merely associative, reading of the claim). Plausible confounding would work against the observed effect (if all identifiable biases would be expected to reduce or reverse the observed association, yet the association still holds, this is evidence the claim is more secure than the raw study design would suggest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These upgrade criteria require an explicit, checkable argument (not just intuition) about why confounding cannot plausibly account for the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of recommendation is distinct from certainty of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations are graded strong or weak (also called conditional/discretionary), based on four inputs: quality of evidence, balance of benefits vs. harms/burdens/costs, values and preferences, and resource use/cost-effectiveness of the intervention. A strong recommendation is made when desirable effects clearly outweigh (or clearly do not outweigh) undesirable effects; a weak recommendation is made when trade-offs are closely balanced or evidence is of low certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-supported (high-certainty) claim about a marginal benefit may still only justify a weak recommendation, while a lower-certainty claim about a decisive benefit/harm trade-off can justify a strong one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate certainty per outcome/claim, not per study or review
rubrics_metrics.description: A review can make some well-supported claims and some poorly-supported claims simultaneously - certainty must be assessed per specific outcome/claim, not per study or per review as a whole.
